claims.text: Varying the relative concentrations of magnetic and non-magnetic elements can tune the magnetic ordering of non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys.
Compositionally induced changes in magnetic ordering can tune the magnetocaloric behavior of low-dimensional high-entropy alloys.
The baseline non-equiatomic alloy exhibits a magnetic transition temperature and a magnetocaloric response.
The alloy's magnetic behavior can be modified by changing the concentration of a magnetic element during synthesis.
The distribution of magnetic and non-magnetic atoms mediates local magnetic exchange interactions in the alloy.
Changing alloy composition modulates magnetic exchange pathways.
Changing alloy composition modifies the distribution of local magnetic moments.
Composition-induced changes in exchange pathways and local moments shift the magnetic transition temperature.
Composition-induced changes in exchange pathways and local moments alter the magnetic entropy change during a transition.
Changing composition will systematically shift magnetic properties such as the Curie temperature relative to the baseline alloy.
Changing composition will systematically adjust the magnitude and temperature range of the magnetocaloric effect relative to the baseline alloy.
The proposed composition-tuning relationship applies only over a range in which phase stability is maintained.
Secondary phases or other dominant microstructural changes can override the proposed composition-driven magnetic behavior.
Strain and processing-induced defects could also influence the magnetocaloric response.
The hypothesis has no direct support from the provided evidence records.
